description: Visualizing Bidirectional BFS pathfinding on New York (SoHo)
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — launch two searches and watch them collide ⚡

Imagine you want to find the fastest path from your start to your destination across a grid-like city map.
✅ Normal BFS expands outward from START only.
✅ Bidirectional BFS expands from START and from GOAL at the same time.

The magic is the meeting condition:
- Keep two frontiers: forwardQueue and backwardQueue
- Maintain visited sets for each direction
- Each step expands the smaller frontier (fastest in practice)
- Stop when a node appears in BOTH visited sets

Why it’s faster:
If the solution is depth d and the branching factor is b, one-way BFS explores ~b^d nodes. Bidirectional BFS splits the depth into ~b^(d/2) from each side, cutting the search space dramatically.

Coding interview takeaway: “Meeting in the middle” is the same concept behind many graph optimizations—reduce effective depth, not just runtime constants.

Debate question: Should you always expand the smaller frontier, or is simple two-sided expansion “good enough” in interviews?

yt_description:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half (real map routing) ⚡

In this Short, we visualize Bidirectional BFS on a Barcelona (Eixample)-style grid: two simultaneous searches expand from START and GOAL, then stop instantly when the frontiers meet. This is the core of bidirectional bfs explained—meeting in the middle to cut the search space roughly from ~b^d to ~2*b^(d/2).

Mechanics:
1) forwardQueue + forwardVisited
2) backwardQueue + backwardVisited
3) expand each turn (best practice: expand the smaller frontier)
4) terminate when a node is visited from both sides
